name: Great Hall, Winchester Castle
text: Your train passes near the Great Hall of Winchester Castle, on the train's {side}, all that stands of the castle William the Conqueror founded in 1067 besides its Westgate. On its wall hangs the Round Table, made in the 13th century and repainted for Henry VIII, whose young face is King Arthur's.

name: Shawford Down
text: Your train passes near Shawford Down, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of chalk grassland. Its slopes still show strip lynchets, terraces left from the Middle Ages, when it was ploughed as common land.

name: Eastleigh
text: Your train passes near the middle of Eastleigh, on the train's {side}, a town that grew up in the 1800s around the London and South Western Railway. A Saxon village called East Leah was recorded here as long ago as 932.

name: King John's House, Romsey
text: Your train passes near King John's House in Romsey, on the train's {side}, said to have been King John's hunting lodge. It was in fact built in 1256, some 40 years after he died, though some of its beams may come from an older building.

name: Southampton Airport
text: Your train passes Southampton Airport, on the train's {side}, where the prototype Spitfire made its first flight on March 5th 1936. A two-thirds-size model of it, K5054, stands at the road entrance.

name: St Mary's Church, South Stoneham
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at South Stoneham, on the train's {side}, one of the two medieval churches left in Southampton. Parts of it are Norman, and its chancel arch dates from the 1100s.

name: South Stoneham House
text: Your train passes near South Stoneham House, on the train's {side}, an early 18th-century manor house thought to be by Nicholas Hawksmoor. What is now the University of Southampton bought it in 1921 for students and added a 17-storey tower in 1964; it has stood empty since 2005.

name: Eastleigh Works
text: Your train passes Eastleigh Works, on the train's {side}, opened by the London and South Western Railway in 1891 to build carriages and wagons. Locomotive building moved here from Nine Elms in London in 1910.

name: Shamblehurst Farmhouse
text: Your train passes near Shamblehurst Farmhouse, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house partly from the 1600s, its upper floor jutting out over the lower. It now goes by the name Strawberry Cottage.

name: Funtley Deviation
text: Your train passes the old Funtley Deviation, on the train's {side}, a two-mile line opened in 1904 to avoid the unstable Fareham tunnel. It had troubles of its own, and closed in May 1973, when trains went back through the tunnel; it is now a footpath.

name: Basing House
text: Your train passes near Basing House, on the train's {side}, a Tudor palace built from 1531 for William Paulet, Marquess of Winchester, that once rivalled Hampton Court. Cromwell's troops stormed it in October 1645 after a long siege, and local people were encouraged to carry off its bricks.

name: Hook Common and Bartley Heath
text: Your train passes near Hook Common and Bartley Heath, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest with large areas of wet heath, a habitat that rarely survives in the Thames Basin.

name: Elvetham Heath nature reserve
text: Your train passes near the Elvetham Heath nature reserve, on the train's {side}, where heather and gorse are coming back by themselves. Its wet woodland has bog myrtle, a rare plant.

name: Fleet Pond
text: Your train passes Fleet Pond, on the train's {side}, a fishery first recorded in 1324. The London and Southampton Railway bought it for £50 in the 1830s because it stood in the way, and built an embankment across its northern end.

name: Basingstoke Canal
text: Your train runs beside the Basingstoke Canal, on the train's {side}, finished in 1794 to link Basingstoke with the Thames. It never made money, became derelict, and was reopened in 1991 after years of restoration.

name: Brookwood American Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Brookwood American Cemetery, on the train's {side}, the only American military cemetery of the First World War in the British Isles. Its chapel, opened in 1929, bears the names of 563 missing, most of them lost at sea.

name: Aldershot Military Cemetery
text: Your train passes near Aldershot Military Cemetery, on the train's {side}, laid out in the 1850s when the Army made Aldershot its permanent training base. Nearly 17,000 service people of nine nations are buried there.

name: Badshot Lea Long Barrow
text: Your train passes near the site of Badshot Lea Long Barrow, on the train's {side}, an earthen burial mound probably built more than 5,000 years ago, the only long barrow known in Surrey. Little was left by 1936, when it was excavated because a chalk quarry was about to swallow the rest.

name: William Cobbett pub, Farnham
text: Your train passes near the William Cobbett pub in Farnham, on the train's {side}, once the Jolly Farmer, where the radical writer and MP William Cobbett was born in 1763. It was renamed after him.

name: St Lawrence's Church, Alton
text: Your train passes near St Lawrence's Church in Alton, on the train's {side}, probably begun not long after 1066. On December 13th 1643, in the Civil War, Royalist soldiers made their last stand in it before Parliament's troops broke through the west door.

name: Holy Trinity Church, Aldershot
text: Your train passes near Holy Trinity Church in Aldershot, on the train's {side}, built between 1875 and 1878, the first new church in a town that had grown fast once the Army arrived in the 1850s.

name: Frimley Green Windmill
text: Your train passes near Frimley Green Windmill, on the train's {side}, a brick tower mill first recorded in 1784. From 1803 it belonged to the Royal Military College at Sandhurst; it stopped work by 1870 and became a house in 1914.

name: Staff College, Camberley
text: Your train passes near the old Staff College at Camberley, on the train's {side}, which trained the Army's staff officers until 1997. It grew out of a college opened in High Wycombe in 1799.

name: Camberley Obelisk
text: Your train passes near the Camberley Obelisk, on the train's {side}, which is really a square brick tower, built on a wooded hill in about 1765 to 1770 by the merchant John Norris. It once stood much taller.

name: Bagshot Park
text: Your train passes along Bagshot Park, on the train's {side}, a royal home whose house was built in 1879 for Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught. An earlier lodge here was rebuilt for Charles I by Inigo Jones.

name: Englemere House
text: Your train passes near Englemere House, on the train's {side}, an Italianate house of about 1815 that was the home of Field Marshal Lord Roberts from 1903 until his death in 1914.

name: RAF Staff College, Bracknell
text: Your train passes near the former RAF Staff College at Bracknell, on the train's {side}, where the Royal Air Force trained its staff officers from 1945 to 1997, in a Victorian house called Ramslade House.

name: Ranelagh School
text: Your train passes near Ranelagh School in Bracknell, on the train's {side}, a Church of England school founded by Lord Ranelagh in 1709.

name: Charters House
text: Your train passes near Charters, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco house built in 1938 for the industrialist Frank Parkinson. His guests included Winston Churchill and the Duke and Duchess of Windsor.

name: Bromhall Priory
text: Your train passes near the site of Bromhall Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Benedictine nuns from 1200. The Pope suppressed it in 1524, and its lands went to St John's College, Cambridge.

name: Longcross Studios
text: Your train passes near Longcross Studios, on the train's {side}, opened in 2006 where military vehicles were tested from 1942 to 2005 and Chobham armour was developed. The James Bond film Skyfall was made here.

name: Holloway Sanatorium
text: Your train passes near the old Holloway Sanatorium, on the train's {side}, built between 1873 and 1885 for the philanthropist Thomas Holloway to treat people with temporary mental illness. Pevsner called it and its sister, Royal Holloway College, the summit of High Victorian design; it is now homes.

name: St Ann's Hill
text: Your train passes near St Ann's Hill, on the train's {side}, the highest point in Chertsey. Its summit was a key viewing point for the survey of the 1780s that linked the Greenwich and Paris observatories by a chain of triangles.

name: Chertsey Abbey
text: Your train passes near the site of Chertsey Abbey, on the train's {side}, founded in 666 by Saint Erkenwald. King Henry VI was buried here before his body was moved to St George's Chapel, Windsor.

name: Coxes Lock
text: Your train passes near Coxes Lock on the Wey Navigation, on the train's {side}, built between 1651 and 1653. Its mill pond is the biggest on the navigation, and its old mill buildings are now flats.

name: Concorde G-BBDG, Brooklands Museum
text: Your train passes near Brooklands Museum, on the train's {side}, home to Concorde G-BBDG, built for testing before the planes carried passengers. It first flew in February 1974, last flew on Christmas Eve 1981, and came here by road in 2003.

name: Brooklands
text: Your train passes near Brooklands, on the train's {side}, opened in 1907 as the world's first purpose-built banked motor racing circuit, and one of Britain's first airfields. Its last race was in August 1939.

name: Shah Jahan Mosque
text: Your train passes near the Shah Jahan Mosque in Woking, on the train's {side}, the first purpose-built mosque in the United Kingdom, finished in 1889. A ship's captain was brought in to take the bearings that line it up with Mecca.

name: Brookwood Cemetery
text: Your train passes Brookwood Cemetery, on the train's {side}, the largest in the United Kingdom, opened in 1854 for London's dead. Coffins and mourners came out from a special station beside Waterloo, on a branch line into the cemetery.

name: Smart's and Prey Heaths
text: Your train passes near Smart's and Prey Heaths, on the train's {side}, damp heaths of ling and purple moor-grass where two kinds of sundew, small plants that catch insects, grow.
